core_idea: **Make** means cause something to exist, to happen, or to be a certain way, and many common actions are expressed with **make** and a noun.

senses.definition: produce something that did not exist before, for example by putting parts together, by cooking, or by writing

examples.text: Mari made a cake for the party.
Sam made us all a cup of tea.
The table is made of solid wood.
Yuki makes short films about city life.

synonyms.note: **build** is for houses, walls, and other large structures
**manufacture** is for factory production in large numbers

subsenses.definition: cause something such as a mark, a hole, a sound, or a mess to appear

examples.text: Try not to make a mess in the kitchen.
The children were making a lot of noise upstairs.
The nail made a small hole in the wall.

adaptation.semantic: English uses **make** alike for cooking food, building things, and producing works of art. Many languages prefer a specific verb for each, such as **cook**, **build**, or **write**; those verbs exist in English too, but the general word is always acceptable.
adaptation.grammar: The person who receives what is made can come before it as a second object: *make me a sandwich*, the same as *make a sandwich for me*. Many languages need a preposition or a different word order here.

senses.definition: perform the action that the following noun names, for example a decision, a mistake, a promise, or a telephone call
senses.explanation: **Make** carries little meaning of its own here; the noun carries it. Which nouns take **make** and which take **do** has to be learned one by one: *you make a decision but do your homework*.

examples.text: We need to make a decision by Friday.
Everyone makes mistakes when they are learning something new.
They made us a very good offer for the house.
Can I make a suggestion?

compare.note: do is for tasks and activities: do the dishes, do some work, do your homework
take a photo, take a shower, take a test
have a party, have a meal, have a rest

adaptation.semantic: Many languages use one verb where English chooses between **make** and **do**, or use a different light verb, such as **give**, **take**, or **have**, with the same noun. Learn each noun with its verb: *make a decision*, *do the dishes*, *take a photo*, *have a party*.

senses.definition: cause someone or something to be in a certain state, or to become a certain thing

examples.text: The long walk made everyone hungry.
Loud music makes it hard to think.
examples.note: **it** stands for the phrase that follows

examples.text: The club made Ana its new leader.
Speak slowly so that you make yourself understood.

items: make it easy for someone to do something

subsenses.definition: change something so that it becomes something different

examples.text: They made the old barn into a house.
You could make this long dress into a skirt.

adaptation.grammar: The new state comes straight after the object with no linking word: *make someone happy*, not *make someone to be happy* or *make someone as happy*. With a phrase or clause as the object, it stands in first: *make it clear that you disagree*.

senses.definition: force or cause someone to do something, or cause something to happen

examples.text: My parents made me clean my room before I could go out.
Onions always make me cry.
What made you change your mind?
We were made to wait outside in the cold.

synonyms.note: **force** is stronger and takes **to**: *force someone to do something*

compare.note: *let someone do something* means allow, with the same bare infinitive
*get someone to do something* means persuade, and keeps **to**

adaptation.grammar: In the active, the verb after the object has no **to**: *she made him wait*. In the passive, **to** returns: *he was made to wait*. Many languages use a special causative form or a that-clause here; English never says *make that someone does something*.

senses.definition: earn or gain money, especially by working or by doing business

examples.text: How much do you make a month?
The store made a small profit this year.
Lee makes a living by fixing bicycles.
They made a lot of money when they sold the house.

synonyms.note: **earn** and **make** are both common in writing; **make** is the usual word for a business's profit or a stated wage

senses.definition: be equal to a total when numbers or amounts are put together

examples.text: Three and four make seven.
With Omar, that makes eight people for dinner.
examples.note: bringing a count up to a total

examples.text: That makes the third time you have been late this week.

subsenses.definition: calculate or judge something to be a certain amount or time

examples.text: I make it just after nine.
What do you make the total?

senses.definition: have the qualities needed to be or to become a certain thing

examples.text: Sara will make a wonderful doctor.
This little room would make a nice office.
You two would make a great team.

adaptation.grammar: The noun after **make** here describes the subject, not an object: *she will make a good teacher* means she will be one. There is no passive and no continuous form.

senses.definition: manage to arrive at a place or to be present at an event, especially by a certain time

examples.text: We ran and just made the last train.
Can you make the meeting on Thursday?
If we leave now, we should make the airport by six.
I have a lot to do, but I will try to make the deadline.

subsenses.definition: manage to get a place on a team or on a list, or to appear in the news

examples.text: Kim made the school team this year.
The story made the front page of the local paper.
Only three of the songs made the final list.

senses.definition: understand something in a certain way, or form an opinion about it

examples.text: What do you make of the new manager?
I couldn't make anything of the map.
Nobody knew what to make of her silence.

items: what do you make of something
not know what to make of something

adaptation.grammar: Always with **of** after the object, and the object is **what**, **nothing**, **anything**, **much**, or **little**: *what do you make of it?* It is used mostly in questions and negatives.

phrases.definition: check that something is true or has been done, or act so that something certainly happens
phrases.explanation: Followed by a that-clause, usually without **that** in speech (*make sure the door is locked*), or by **of** and a noun (*make sure of a seat*). **Make certain** means the same and is a little more formal.

examples.text: Make sure you lock the door when you leave.
I called to make sure that the store was open.
We arrived early to make sure of a good seat.

adaptation.grammar: The clause after **make sure** normally takes the present simple for future time: *make sure you are there at six*, rarely *will be there*.

phrases.definition: arrive in time, manage to do something difficult, or stay alive after an illness or an accident
phrases.explanation: The meaning depends on the situation: *make it to a meeting* (arrive), *make it as a singer* (succeed), or, of a sick person, *be expected to make it* (live). **Make it big** means become very successful.

examples.text: We left late but still made it to the airport in time.
Not many young players make it as professionals.
The doctors say she is going to make it.

adaptation.semantic: Three uses that most languages express with three different verbs: **arrive**, **succeed**, and **survive**.

phrases.definition: manage with something that is not as good or as much as you would like
phrases.explanation: The with-phrase can be left out when it is clear what is meant: *there is no milk, so we will have to make do*.

examples.text: There was no bread, so we made do with crackers.
We can't afford a new car, so we'll make do with the old one for another year.

phrases.definition: get as much benefit or enjoyment as possible from something, especially something that will not last
phrases.explanation: **Make the best of something** is similar but is used for a bad situation that you accept and try to improve.

examples.text: It's a beautiful day, so make the most of it.
She made the most of her year abroad by traveling every weekend.

phrases.text: make or break someone or something
phrases.definition: be the thing that decides whether someone or something has complete success or complete failure
phrases.explanation: Often used before a noun: *a make-or-break decision*.

examples.text: The next game will make or break the team's season.
This year could make or break the company.

phrases.definition: become successful and respected through your own efforts

examples.text: Her parents wanted her to go to college and make something of herself.
He left the village at eighteen, determined to make something of himself.

phrases.definition: do what you promised or threatened to do, or pay what you owe
phrases.explanation: The object is a promise, a threat, or a debt: *make good on a promise*, *make good on a loan*.

examples.text: The company made good on its promise to refund every customer.
He made good on his threat to leave.

phrases.definition: act as if something were true, especially as a game
phrases.explanation: Followed by a that-clause. As a noun or an adjective, **make-believe** means pretending: *a world of make-believe*.

examples.text: The children made believe that the sofa was a boat.
Let's make believe we're explorers in the jungle.

synonym_discrimination.note: **Do** is for activities, work, and tasks, and for the nouns that name them: *do the dishes*, *do your homework*, *do some exercise*. **Make** is for producing something that was not there before, and for many fixed noun partners: *make a cake*, *make a decision*, *make a mistake*. When the noun names a result or a new thing, **make** is usually right; when it names an activity, **do** is.

usage_note: **Made of** names a material that you can still see in the finished thing: *a table made of wood*. **Made from** names a material that has been changed: *paper made from wood*, *wine made from grapes*. **Made by** names the maker and **made in** names the place: *made by hand*, *made in a small factory*.

learner_errors.incorrect: My mother made me to clean my room.
learner_errors.correct: My mother made me clean my room.
learner_errors.note: After **make** and an object, the next verb has no **to**; **to** appears only in the passive: *I was made to clean my room*.

learner_errors.incorrect: I have to make my homework.
learner_errors.correct: I have to do my homework.
learner_errors.note: Tasks and activities take **do**; **make** is for producing something new.

learner_errors.incorrect: We made a photo in front of the house.
learner_errors.correct: We took a photo in front of the house.
learner_errors.note: Photos are **taken**, not made; a party is **had** or **given**, and exercise is **done**.

adaptation.semantic: **Make** covers producing, causing, and a large set of fixed noun partners such as *make a decision*. Many languages have one verb for **make** and **do**, or split producing (**build**, **cook**) from causing. The senses here mark the places where the translation changes.
adaptation.grammar: **Make** plus object plus bare infinitive in the active (*made him wait*) becomes *made to wait* in the passive. The second object (*make me a coffee*) and the state after the object (*make it clear*) both stand without a preposition.
adaptation.pronunciation: The vowel is the long **a** of **day** and the final **e** is silent, so **make** rhymes with **cake**. The past tense **made** rhymes with **paid**, and its final **d** is fully pronounced.
